client: It's been six months since I lost Sam to cancer, and I still can't seem to move forward. Everyone keeps telling me I should be "getting better" by now, but all my favorite things just feel empty without them. I tried going out with friends last weekend, but I just sat there feeling completely disconnected while everyone else was laughing and having fun.
therapist:
It sounds like you're carrying a deep sadness that makes the world feel colorless without Sam, and the pressure to "move on" is adding its own weight. When you describe feeling disconnected even among friends, I hear both the grief and how isolating it can feel when others don't share your emotional reality right now. 

Would it feel accurate to say that part of the struggle is this tension between missing Sam deeply and feeling like you "should" be somewhere else emotionally by now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
Yeah, that's exactly it. I feel guilty when people say things like "They wouldn't want you to be sad" because of course Sam wouldn't, but that doesn't just magically make the sadness disappear. And then I get angry at myself for still crying over old photos when it's been half a year already. 

Part of me knows grief doesn't have a timeline, but the other part keeps comparing myself to how my cousin "bounced back" after her loss. It makes me feel broken.
therapist:
The way your voice tightens as you speak tells me how deeply this guilt and self-judgment are weighing on you - it's like you're holding two truths at once: your natural grief, and this punishing expectation of where you "should" be.  

When you compare yourself to your cousin, I wonder if we might examine that thought - what evidence do we have that her grief journey is the "right" way, rather than just being different from yours?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client:
I guess I don't really know how my cousin is truly feeling inside - she just seems so together on the surface. But even if her grief is different, it's hard not to feel like I'm failing somehow. Every time I try to push myself to be more "normal," I just end up feeling worse, like I'm betraying Sam's memory by pretending I'm okay. 

Sometimes I wonder if I'm just holding onto the grief too tightly because letting it go feels like letting Sam go all over again.
therapist:
Your voice sounds both weary and urgent as you share this - like the grief is this heavy weight you're carrying, yet there's also fear about what might happen if you set it down even briefly. That tension between holding on and letting go sounds exhausting to navigate alone.  

It might help to gently challenge that thought that grieving differently = failing - what if honoring your unique process is actually the most authentic way to keep Sam's memory alive?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client:
That idea about honoring my process being authentic... it makes sense intellectually, but my stomach still clenches when I think about it. What if my way of grieving isn't actually helping me? What if I'm just making excuses for being stuck? 

I keep thinking about how Sam was always the strong one who pushed through hard times - and here I am falling apart over something they can't even help me with anymore. That thought alone makes me feel so ashamed.
therapist:
The way your voice speeds up and rises tells me how much distress these thoughts are causing you - it's like you're caught between believing you should be strong like Sam and feeling overwhelmed by the very real pain of missing them.  

When you say "falling apart," I hear how you're judging your grief by Sam's strength, but might we consider that what made Sam so special to you was their ability to see and accept you exactly as you are - including in moments of vulnerability?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client:
That last part hit hard... Sam did always seem to understand me in a way no one else did. They'd probably be the first to tell me to stop being so hard on myself. But even thinking that makes me tear up because I can't hear their voice saying it anymore. 

I want to believe they'd accept me as I am now, but it's just so hard to feel their presence when the grief feels so heavy all the time.
therapist:
The way your voice quivers and speeds up tells me how deeply you're feeling both the loss of Sam's physical presence and their unique ability to comfort you. It's clear their understanding meant everything to you, and now that absence feels especially sharp when you need that reassurance most.  

Perhaps we could explore ways to reconnect with Sam's voice - not literally, but through the values and wisdom they shared with you that still live within your memories?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I like the idea of reconnecting with Sam's voice, but it also makes me nervous. What if I try to remember their wisdom and I just end up feeling worse because it reminds me of what I've lost? I keep thinking about this journal Sam used to write in - it's still on their nightstand - but every time I consider opening it, I freeze up. Maybe it's better to leave it untouched.
therapist:
I hear both hopeful curiosity and nervous energy in your voice as you talk about the journal - like part of you wants to reach for that connection while another part is bracing for the pain it might bring.  

That hesitation makes so much sense - it's as if the journal holds both the comfort of Sam's presence and the fresh ache of their absence. Would it feel possible to explore this gently, perhaps starting with just holding the journal before deciding whether to open it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
Just holding it first... that actually feels manageable. But what if I break down completely when I touch it? Last time I tried to move one of Sam's things, I had to leave the room because I couldn't stop sobbing. 

Part of me worries that if I start engaging with their belongings this way, I'll just fall apart and never put myself back together again.
therapist:
Your voice trembles with both determination and fear as you describe this - it's clear the journal represents so much more than just pages, and the thought of opening that floodgate of emotion feels terrifying right now.  

That worry about breaking down completely makes perfect sense, and yet I notice the careful wisdom in your suggestion to start small - perhaps we could plan together how to create moments of safety before and after touching the journal, so you feel more anchored?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
Having a safety plan does sound comforting, but I'm still scared of what might come up. What if I start crying and can't stop? I've been trying to keep it together for so long that the thought of letting go feels like opening a dam that might flood everything. 

Maybe I need more time before I'm ready to even hold the journal. It's just... I don't know how long "enough time" is supposed to be.
therapist:
I hear both the fear in your rapid words and a glimmer of something else - maybe cautious hope? - beneath the surface as you consider this step. That image of the dam shows how powerfully you've been holding everything back, and how overwhelming it feels to contemplate releasing it.  

Let's honor your wisdom in recognizing you might need more time - there's no rush here. Would it help if we explored what "feeling ready" might look like for you, rather than chasing some external timeline?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
I don't even know what "ready" would feel like anymore. Every time I think I might be getting there, I remember how Sam's sweater still smells like them, or find their favorite coffee mug in the cabinet, and it knocks me right back down. 

Part of me wants to believe I'll know when I'm ready, but another part worries that day will never come. Maybe I'm just too afraid to face how much this still hurts.
therapist:
The way your voice rises and quickens tells me how raw these memories still feel - how those everyday moments with Sam's things can suddenly bring the loss crashing back with such force. It sounds exhausting to keep getting knocked down just when you think you might be finding your footing.  

That fear about never feeling ready is completely understandable, and yet I notice something important - even in this pain, you're showing up to examine these feelings rather than avoiding them completely. That takes remarkable courage, even if it doesn't feel like it right now.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client:
It doesn't feel like courage though - it just feels like surviving. And honestly, sometimes I wonder if even that is worth it. The pain of missing Sam is so constant that most days I just go through the motions, waiting for time to pass. 

I know you're trying to help me see strength in this, but right now all I feel is tired. Tired of hurting, tired of trying, tired of pretending I believe it'll ever get better.
therapist:
The heaviness in your voice and the way your words slow down tell me how completely exhausted you are by this grief - it's not just emotional pain but a physical weariness that makes even surviving feel like too much some days.  

When you say it doesn't feel like courage, I hear how the effort of simply continuing feels invisible to you right now - and yet here you are, still showing up to this painful work when every part of you wants to turn away. That's not just survival; that's the quietest, most honest kind of bravery.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
